p: Henry ran his daughter's science fair trick on the claim, counting the first digit of every fraud payment, and the nines stood far too tall.
Most of the extra nines sat in that cluster just under the approval line.
Maisie caught a mistake in his chart, one row too many, and he fixed it in the open with her name in his notes.
Meridian's record of four days of settlements, nearly three billion dollars, tied to his own count to the cent.
He made it to the science fair. Then Lou texted. Dot had a State Capitol tour map in her handbag, with the mile high step circled in green.
Lou Mancuso. The detective. He's started bringing Henry copies.
Giles Fenwick. Henry's boss in London. His board will ask him on Monday whether they pay.
Nkechi Obi. The FBI agent. She knows things about Henry he never told her.
Leonard Pratt. Meridian's director of internal audit. Cheerful, quick, and keen to help.
Maisie Ashby. Henry's daughter. She's started ringing him.
New in this chapter: Simon Kade.

The west steps of the State Capitol face the mountains, which is lovely at sunset and no use at all at twenty past six on a Friday morning in March, when the sun is still somewhere behind the building and the granite has held on to the whole night's cold. Henry Ashby stood at the bottom with his hands in his coat pockets.

He'd walked past these steps for eleven months. This morning he went up them, one at a time, counting out loud like a man checking his change. On the thirteenth he found a small brass marker. On the fifteenth, cut into the face of the step in letters worn soft at the edges, were the words ONE MILE ABOVE SEA LEVEL. The seventeenth carried the newest mark of all, from last summer's survey. The eighteenth had another brass marker, older and duller. Four steps, each of them a mile high, and no two of them the same step.

Lou Mancuso came up from Colfax at half past with two coffees and a manila envelope under his arm. He handed Henry a coffee, then the envelope. Copies. Like I said. Don't make me regret the 'like I said.'
Inside was a photocopy of the folded tour map from Dot's handbag, flattened out, with her green circle around one paragraph. Inside the circle she'd underlined the four years, each one twice.

State Capitol tour map, photocopy, Dot's green circle. The Mile High Steps. In 1909 the words "One Mile Above Sea Level" were carved into the 15th step. In 1969 a survey by Colorado State University students put the mile high point on the 18th step. In 2003 a more precise survey moved it to the 13th. In 2026 a new federal survey moved it again, to the 17th.
So which one's right? Lou said.
All of them. In their year.

The step never moved. What changed was what they measured it against. Henry looked up at the dome, which was just beginning to catch the light. Every marker was true the day somebody set it. Nobody went back and took the old ones out.

Lou drank some coffee and thought about it. Then he said, as if it were the same subject, Her name's been bugging me since Tuesday. Kessler. I looked it up last night. Two thousand nine, Denver District Court. State case against an officer at a little state chartered bank. I worked the money side of it. She was the regulator's witness. He smiled for the first time since Henry had known him. Defense counsel asked her had she ever missed anything, in all those years. She said, 'Once.' Counsel was so surprised they forgot to ask when. The jury loved her.
Henry wrote it in his notebook, word for word, with the year. Lou watched him do it and didn't say anything, which Henry was starting to understand was approval.

On the walk back down Sixteenth Street, he made a list in his head. He went into a drugstore for a notepad and came out with a box of green pens. He didn't ask himself why. At the office he wrote it on the whiteboard, under the shopping list nobody had erased. First the four steps and their years: the fifteenth, 1909. The eighteenth, 1969. The thirteenth, 2003. The seventeenth, 2026. Then, beside them, the markers in the claim pack. Leonard's controls report, signed in 2026. Hollins and Pike's opinion, as of December 31, 2026. Every document in the claim pack that said the capstone worked was a marker on a step, and every one had a year on it. Check the year, she'd written. He didn't know yet which year she meant. He knew where to start looking: at the people who were supposed to check.

The radiator was knocking like someone who wanted to be let in when Henry turned to page 12 of the claim pack. It was Meridian's organization chart. He'd looked at it on Tuesday. This time he read it.

Meridian's organization chart. Simon Kade, the founder, chairs the board, which has a three director audit committee, and he's the chief executive too, with Carla Wynn, the CFO, reporting to him. Reporting to the CFO are settlement operations, finance and reconciliation, the chief information officer, and internal audit under Leonard Pratt, and under the CIO sit information security, database administration, and security monitoring, the system called DOME.
He drew it again on the back of an envelope, with lines instead of boxes, the way Dot used to. All the lines went to the same place.

The reporting line goes at the top of a clean page. Settlement operations, reconciliation, IT, security, database administration, internal audit: every one of them rolls up to Carla Wynn. The people who run the capstone and the people who check it share a boss. Underneath he writes the question that follows: what did the board hear about any of it, and from whom?

Good governance keeps the people who run a process apart from the people who give assurance over it, and gives the assurance functions a line to the board. When one executive owns the process, the systems, security, and internal audit, nobody independent of that executive reports on the key control.

Just after nine, Vellacott's counsel forwarded what he'd asked for on Wednesday: Meridian's board and audit committee minutes for 2025 and 2026. Eight quarters. He read every page, then made a table of them on a legal pad.

Henry's notes: audit committee minutes, Q1 2025 to Q4 2026. Meetings held: 8 of 8. Present every time: three directors; S. Kade (Chairman, by invitation); C. Wynn (CFO). Internal audit: not present at any meeting, not on any agenda. Session without management present: none recorded. IT or security on the agenda: once, Q2 2025, "DOME dashboard: noted."
One name sat in all eight meetings, by invitation. The chairman, who was also the chief executive, who was also the man the CFO reported to. Henry underlined it once and turned the page.

On Tuesday he'd written that his reliance on Leonard's work was limited, pending review. Here was the review. For two years, the only person who'd told Meridian's audit committee anything about controls was the CFO whose systems they were.

He writes it plainly: no meeting between internal audit and the audit committee in eight quarters, no private session, a charter approved by the CFO alone. Then, in the reliance column for Leonard's 2026 report, he crosses out what he'd written there on Tuesday and writes "none." He doesn't enjoy it. Leonard has been nothing but helpful. That was rather the problem.

An audit committee should oversee internal audit and meet the chief audit executive, including without management present. A function that never reaches those charged with governance has no independent line to them, and its work can't be relied on without one.

Next he opened the folder Leonard had sent on Wednesday under the subject line Everything you need on authorization! It held three documents. He laid them out side by side on the desk, oldest on the left.

Settlement authorization: the three documents. Settlement Authorization Policy. Approved by the Board, March 2019. "All outgoing settlements shall be authorized in accordance with the Settlement Authorization Standard. This policy is reviewed annually." Settlement Authorization Standard. Approved by the CFO, 2019. "Settlement files above $10,000 require approval by a second authorized user who did not prepare the file." Desk Procedure SO-14, revised January 2026. "Step 6. Second approver confirms the file total and releases."

The standard says the second approver must be someone who didn't prepare the file. The procedure, revised in January 2026, says only that the second approver confirms the total and releases. The words about who may approve didn't make it down the ladder. Then the years: a policy that requires an annual review, approved in March 2019. Reviews were due every March from 2020 to 2026. That's seven at least, and the file holds none. He writes check the year in the margin, and then feels slightly foolish, and leaves it.

Policies, standards, and procedures should agree, from intent down to the steps at the desk. Trace each requirement down the ladder and note where it changes, and check each document's approval and review dates against what it says about itself.

The last thing in Leonard's folder was Meridian's policy exception register, a spreadsheet of nineteen rows going back to 2019. Most were dull: a laptop standard waived for a contractor, a password rule relaxed for a printer. One wasn't.

Policy exception register (extract). EX-2022-07. Quarterly review of the authorized approver list, Settlement Authorization Standard section 4: suspended for Q3 and Q4 2022 due to staffing. Requested by: Settlement Operations. Approved by: C. Wynn, CFO. Compensating control: none stated. Expiry: none stated. Status: OPEN.
He checked the review log for the approver list. The last review was dated June 2022.

It's a finding: a quarterly review of who may approve settlements, suspended in 2022 for two quarters, never restarted, no end date, nothing to compensate, signed off by the CFO whose department asked for it. Then he adds the approver list to the request list as well, because the finding tells him exactly where to test next.

An exception is a risk acceptance. It's approved by the risk owner with the authority to accept it, not by the person who asked, and it carries a stated reason, a compensating control, and an end date. An exception without an end date has quietly become the policy.
Meridian's risk register was at the back of the Q4 2026 board pack, in an appendix nobody had bothered to number. Row seven was the one that mattered.

Meridian Clearing, enterprise risk register, row R-07. Risk: unauthorized or fraudulent settlement. Owner: CFO. Inherent: likelihood 4, impact 5, score 20. Key control: dual authorization (assessed effective, 2019 control assessment). Residual: likelihood 1, impact 5, score 5 (LOW). Board appetite: residual score above 8 requires a treatment plan reported to the board. Last reviewed: 2019. Next review: 2020.
The settlement platform described in the claim pack had been built in 2019. He wrote a question he couldn't answer yet.

Nothing else holds it up. The residual score of 5 rests on a control assessment from 2019, never repeated, for a risk that scores 20 without the control. That score sits under the board's line of 8, so the board was never shown a treatment plan, and never asked for one. The register was due for review in 2020. He circles 2019 in green, then stops and looks at the pen.

Residual risk depends on controls working, and controls have to be retested, especially when systems change. A rating whose basis is years old isn't evidence of current risk. Record the gap and the reason, and don't substitute your own rating as fact.
At 11:05 Giles rang from a taxi. It was five past six in London, and he sounded as if the taxi were going somewhere he was looking forward to.

Quick thought for your view, Henry. Meridian bought our policy, so the risk's been transferred, hasn't it? Their board can rate things however it likes. Once they've insured it, it's ours. So their governance is rather beside the point, surely.

Insurance moves the cost. Their board still owned the risk and the control. And we wrote the policy on what they told us about that control. If their own board was rating it on a 2019 test, that matters to us twice. There's a pause with traffic in it. Fair. One paragraph. Plain English, please. The board's had a week of acronyms.

Risk transfer, usually through insurance, shares the financial impact. Accountability for the risk and for the controls stays with the organization's board and management. That's why governance still matters after a risk is insured.
Every director had read this page. You could tell from the coffee ring on Meridian's scanned copy. One page. Four measures. Eight quarters of them, and every box green.

Board pack, IT performance scorecard, Q4 2026. Settlement platform availability: 99.97% (target 99.9%). Daily reconciliations completed: 100% (target 100%). Security alerts triaged within service level: 100% (target 98%). Critical patches applied within 30 days: 96% (target 95%). Source for all measures: DOME. Prepared by: IT.
He read the footer twice. Don't trust the dome.

He writes the questions beside each line. The answers are already mostly on the page. All four come from DOME, all four were prepared by IT, and nobody outside IT checks them. And none of them measures whether the key control did its job. "Reconciliations completed" counts that the reconciliation ran. It doesn't say what it found.

Performance measures are only useful if they're relevant to the goal, clearly defined, and reliably sourced, with someone independent checking them. A scorecard drawn from one system and prepared by the team it measures is that system's view of itself.

Agent Obi rang at half past twelve to say the bureau's formal request for the claim file had gone to Vellacott's counsel that morning. It took her about ninety seconds. Then, in the same even voice, You were Intelligence Corps.
Is that in a file somewhere?
It's in how you stood on your landing on Tuesday. Like you'd already counted the exits. She rang off before he'd decided whether it was a compliment.
The reconciliations arrived after lunch, the ones he'd put at the top of his list on Tuesday. Meridian had sent the sign off sheets for the week of the event.

The sign off sheets for the reconciliation against the Federal Reserve record, where each morning's run covers the day before. On March 2 it finished at 7:41 with no difference. On March 3 it finished at 7:44 and found a difference, and on March 4 at 7:39 it found one again, and both times the disposition was a timing difference, carried forward, initialed by the supervisor, B N. On March 5, the run for March 4's settlements wasn't performed. The incident had been declared at 4:40 that morning.

The sheets say it plainly. The reconciliation ran and found a difference on March 3 and again on March 4, and both times the difference was called timing and carried forward, with no escalation. The board's measure counted only that it ran. Then he sits back. The control Dot taught him to look for had done exactly what it was for, twice, and somebody had initialed it away.

A KPI that counts completion can be perfect while the process fails at its purpose. The measure that matters here is breaks found and resolved, and how. Report the gap between what was measured and what the board needed to know.

He started the interim view itself at ten past two. He'd promised it to Giles by five, Denver time, so it would be the first thing Giles read in the morning. He had a blank page and three hours, and he had a great many things he believed.
The sampling section was easy. Two strata, random selection, seeds written down. It was the governance section that worried him, because it was about people.

He writes the first one as Dot would have. Condition: internal audit didn't attend or report to the audit committee in eight quarters. Criteria: an audit charter approved by those charged with governance, and a functional line to them. Cause: a charter approved only by the CFO, and internal audit reporting to the CFO for everything. Effect: no independent assurance to Meridian's board over the key control, and Vellacott can't rely on internal audit's 2026 report. Then a paragraph headed Not yet tested, which is longer than he'd like and exactly as long as it needs to be.
A complete finding states the condition, the criteria, the cause, and the effect. The report also states its limitations, so readers know how far the conclusions go.
At 3:05 his phone showed a Meridian number. It was Leonard Pratt, and he wasn't cheerful.

Mr. Ashby. I hear you asked for the audit committee minutes. I can guess what you found. A breath. Off the record. If your report says internal audit never met the committee, that's my name on it. I asked to go. Twice. In writing. I kept the emails, for whatever that's worth. Carla said the committee gets what it needs from the CFO's office. I've got a mortgage in Arvada and a boss who reads everything. Could it say 'reporting lines need review'? It's the same thing. It's just kinder.

The finding stays, he says. It's about the structure. The cause in it is the charter and the reporting line, and neither of those is yours. Send me those emails through counsel, and they'll go in beside the finding as management's response, in your own words. A long quiet. Okay, Leonard says. Okay. I can do that. After the call Henry writes in the file: 3:05 PM. L. Pratt, by phone, asked that the finding on audit committee reporting be reworded as "reporting lines need review." Declined. Invited a written response through counsel, with his emails.

When someone asks you to soften a supported finding, keep it, and document who asked, when, and what you decided. Fairness comes through an accurate cause and a written management response included in the report.
At 3:40 Giles rang again. It was twenty to eleven in London, and he was at home, and he didn't sound as though the evening had gone the way the taxi had promised.

Meridian's counsel tried to make something of you and the examiner today. Our general counsel pointed them at the disclosure note on your file from Tuesday. It lasted about four minutes. That's what notes are for. Now. The board.
On Monday they'll ask me one thing. Do we pay. I need one word, Henry. Fraud, or not fraud?

Not yet. I can tell you what we know and when we'll know the rest. He gives it in under a minute. What's known: the governance gaps, the reconciliation breaks waved through, the 2,906 under the line. What isn't: why, and by whom. When: the Federal Reserve totals Monday, sample results the week after next. That's three things, not one word. It's one page. Then put a box at the top of it with what I say to the board, and I'll say exactly that.
Good reporting is clear, timely, and fitted to the reader. An executive summary that states what's supported, what's open, and when it will close gives a decision maker something true to say.

By twenty past four the interim view was nearly done. Three of its facts were about Meridian's own records: the audit committee minutes, the charter's approver, and the dates on the authorization policy. If any of them were wrong, he'd rather know before Giles read them to a board.
Vellacott's counsel rang to ask if he wanted anything sent to Meridian before the weekend.

Counsel sends a one page letter at 4:41: three statements of fact, each with its source, and a request to confirm or correct them in writing by Wednesday. Nothing about settlements, reconciliations, or 3:12 AM. Henry marks those three lines in the interim view facts subject to confirmation and sends it to Giles at 5:02.

The main purpose of discussing findings with management before they're final is to confirm the facts. Do it in writing, through the agreed channel, and limit it to what management needs to check, keeping anything that could prejudice an investigation out of it.
The interim view went at 5:02. It was one page, with a box at the top.

Interim view, Meridian Clearing claim, Friday, March 12, 2027 (not an opinion). Governance: no one independent of the CFO reported to Meridian's board on the key control in 2025 or 2026. Facts sent to Meridian through counsel for confirmation. Detective control: the daily reconciliation found differences on March 3 and March 4. Both were carried forward as timing differences. Data: 2,906 claimed settlements sit just under the second approver line. Cause not yet known. Next: Federal Reserve totals Monday; sample results the week of March 22.

He sat with the window cracked and the bicycle shop's radio coming up through the floor, and went over the day in order. A policy nobody had reviewed since 2019. An exception that never ended. A risk rated on a 2019 test. Two breaks, initialed away. A man in Arvada asking for kinder words. None of it said who had done what. All of it said that nobody whose job was to look had been allowed to.
At 6:05 his phone lit up. Laura.

A text from Laura. Can we get coffee Monday evening? Pearl Street, the place by the bookshop, 7? There's something I need to ask you and I'd rather do it in person. It's not about Maisie. Well. It is a bit.
He wrote Yes. 7. and then sat looking at it, because in eight years she had never asked him for anything in person.
At 10:31 an email arrived that wasn't from counsel.

An email from Simon Kade, Chairman, Meridian Clearing. Subject: Our minutes. Mr. Ashby, I'm told you've been reading our board minutes. I'm sorry. They're very dull, and that's my fault. I'd like to meet you properly. My assistant will find a time next week. S.K.

He read it twice. Then he forwarded it to Vellacott's counsel without replying, and wrote it into the file the way he should have logged Leonard's call: the time, the sender, what it asked, and that he hadn't answered.

Under the shopping list, the steps were still on the whiteboard from the morning, with their years: 1909, 1969, 2003, 2026. Every one had been true when somebody set it. He took one of the new green pens out of the box and wrote a fifth year underneath, the one from the top sheet of Dot's folder. Evidence: see 1994. Then he capped the pen and left it there.
At ten past eleven Maisie rang. It was the first night of spring break, so nobody in Boulder was making her go to bed. Hi, she said, as if ringing him were a thing she did.
Mum texted you. It's not bad. I'm not allowed to say. Then, before he could ask anything: Can I ask something? What was she like? The diner lady.
Her name was Dot, he said.

That was as far as he got. He had the rest of it ready. The green ink, the fork, the sugar packets. And the one that stuck in his throat: every Saturday, before she'd looked at the menu, she'd asked after Maisie.
None of it would come out. The line was open and quiet, and he could hear Laura's kitchen behind it, the dishwasher running, a cupboard door.
Maisie waited. Then she said, quite gently for fourteen, Okay. You can tell me another time. And after a moment, Dot's a good name. It's like a period. Like, that's it, end of sentence.
